newsitem.title: SWEDEN: NATO chief declines to be drawn over Baltics.
newsitem.headline: NATO chief declines to be drawn over Baltics.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana refused to be drawn on Wednesday on the likely success of a bid by the three Baltic nations to join the western alliance.

Although U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said during a Nordic visit last month that he did not think the former Soviet republics of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were ready for membership, Solana adhered firmly to the rule book.
He said no decision had yet been made and no country's bid to join had been ruled out.
"A decision on who will join NATO will be taken by the 16 countries who belong to NATO and nobody else," Solana told a press conference during the first visit by a NATO chief to neutral Sweden.

The neighbouring Baltic states, which declared independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, are in the queue of countries hoping to join the Western security alliance as it expands eastwards from 1999.

All three are nervous of their large, volatile neighbour Russia and are anxious to obtain the security mantle of NATO. The Soviet Union used the Baltics states as its western military flank during the Cold War.
A decision on who will be in the first round of new NATO recruits will be made in the middle of 1997. Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovenia are tipped for entry.
"NATO has not taken any decision on countries that should be invited," Solana said. "The decision will be made in the middle of 1997."

NATO has, however, been pushing a souped up version of its Partnership for Peace, known as Super PFP or PFP Plus, as an alternative for countries not admitted to the 16-member alliance or which do not want to join NATO.
The PFP was set up two years ago and now has 27 member nations.
"I do think no one at the end of the day should feel disappointed," Solana said during a question-and-answer session with Swedish politicians.
"We have to achieve a mechanism where everyone gains," he said. "With the scheme we have in mind that can be achieved. PFP should be the answer for many of these countries."
Solana set aside concerns raised over the Baltic states' current security. "We do not see any threat to any country at the moment," he said.
